title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XLII: The Hoard Brought Out (lines 3058–3136)
part: Fitt XLII · The Hoard Brought Out (lines 3058–3136)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 115–118, lines 3058–3136 (fitt XLII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs gesȳne, þæt se sīð ne ðāh
þām ðe unrihte inne gehȳdde
wrǣte under wealle.
sentences.l: Then it was visible that the journey did not prosper for him who, unrightfully, hid ornaments within, under the wall.
sentences.i: Then it was plain that the venture had not prospered for the one who had wrongfully hidden that treasure under the wall.
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs gesȳne, þæt …’ is ‘then it was visible, that …’: ‘gesȳne’ is an adjective, ‘visible, plain’, and the ‘þæt’ clause says what was plain. ‘Se sīð ne ðāh’ is ‘the journey did not prosper’, ‘ðāh’ being the past of ‘þēon’, ‘thrive’. ‘Þām ðe unrihte inne gehȳdde’ is ‘for him who wrongfully hid within’: ‘þām’ is the dative of the one affected and ‘gehȳdde’ the past of ‘gehȳdan’, ‘hide’. The hider is the dragon, who hoarded what was not his (my reading from the context; Bugge and Holthausen print ‘gehȳðde’, ‘plundered’, which would make the thief the one who failed). ‘Wrǣte’ I take as the accusative plural of ‘wrǣt’, ‘ornament, jewel’. The ‘t’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘wræce’, which would be a form of ‘wræc’ (‘exile, misery’) and does not suit the sense as I read it; the apparatus credits ‘wrǣte’ to the editor it abbreviates ‘Tho.’, and it is printed. The poet’s voice here takes up the curse on the hoard with which the last part ended.

sentences.t:
Weard ǣr ofslōh
fēara sumne;
sentences.l: The guardian had first slain one of few;
sentences.i: The guardian had first struck down one of a few;
sentences.n: ‘Weard’ is the noun ‘guardian’ (the dragon, as in ‘biorges weard’ below), not the verb. ‘Ǣr ofslōh’ is ‘had first slain’: ‘ǣr’ ‘before, first’, with a simple past standing for a pluperfect. ‘Fēara sumne’ is ‘one of few’: ‘sum’ with a genitive plural means ‘one of’, as in ‘eahta sum’ below, and ‘fēara’ is the genitive plural of ‘fēa’, ‘few’. The same idiom stands at 1412, ‘hē fēara sum beforan gengde’, ‘he went before as one of few’. Who the one slain is, and who the few are, the line does not say; I take the man as Beowulf (a guess).

sentences.t:
þā sīo fǣhð gewearð
gewrecen wrāðlīce.
sentences.l: then the feud became avenged, fiercely.
sentences.i: and then the feud was fiercely avenged.
sentences.n: ‘Gewearð gewrecen’ is ‘became avenged’, that is, ‘was avenged’: ‘gewearð’ is the past of ‘gewurðan’, ‘become’, and ‘gewrecen’ the participle of ‘gewrecan’, ‘avenge’; ‘sīo fǣhð’, ‘the feud’, is the subject. ‘Wrāðlīce’ is an adverb, ‘angrily, fiercely, grievously’. The feud is the quarrel between the dragon and the Geats, and the vengeance is the killing of the dragon.

sentences.t:
Wundur hwār þonne
eorl ellenrōf ende gefēre
līfgesceafta, þonne leng ne mæg
mon mid his (mā)gum meduseld būan.
sentences.l: A wonder it is where then a valor-bold earl may reach the end of his life-fates, when a man may no longer dwell in the mead-hall with his kinsmen.
sentences.i: It is a thing to wonder at where a valiant man will meet the end of his appointed days, when he may no longer live in the mead-hall among his kinsmen.
sentences.n: ‘Wundur hwār’ is ‘a wonder where’: ‘wundur’ is a noun, ‘marvel’, with ‘is’ understood, and ‘hwār’ is ‘where’, introducing an indirect question; I read it as ‘it is a thing to marvel at where …’, i.e. nobody can tell. ‘Gefēre’ is a present subjunctive of ‘gefēran’, ‘reach’, because it stands in an indirect question. ‘Ende līfgesceafta’ is ‘end of life-fates’: ‘gesceaft’ is something ordained, so the destinies allotted to one life. ‘Ellenrōf’ is ‘valor-bold’ (‘ellen’ ‘valour’, ‘rōf’ ‘bold, stout’). ‘Meduseld’ is ‘mead-hall’ (‘medu’ and ‘seld’, ‘hall’), the place of feasting and companionship; ‘būan’ is ‘dwell in’. The ‘mā’ of ‘(mā)gum’ is in round brackets because the manuscript is lost there; Kemble restored it, giving ‘māgum’, ‘with his kinsmen’. The thought is general, but it describes Beowulf, who did not choose where he would die.

sentences.t:
Swā wæs Bīowulfe, þā hē biorges weard
sōhte searonīðas; seolfa ne cūðe,
þurh hwæt his worulde gedāl weorðan sceolde.
sentences.l: So it was for Beowulf, when he sought the barrow’s guardian, cunning-hatreds; he himself did not know through what his parting from the world should come about.
sentences.i: So it was with Beowulf when he went to seek out the barrow’s keeper and his treacherous malice; he himself did not know by what means his parting from this world was to come.
sentences.n: ‘Swā wæs Bīowulfe’ is ‘so it was for Beowulf’, a dative. ‘Biorges weard’ is ‘guardian of the barrow’, the dragon (compare ‘beorges weard’ in earlier parts). ‘Biorges weard’ and ‘searonīðas’ are both objects of ‘sōhte’, set side by side with no ‘and’. ‘Searonīðas’ is ‘cunning-hatreds’ (‘searu’ ‘craft, treachery’, ‘nīð’ ‘hostility’), accusative plural, the object of ‘sōhte’: he sought out the dragon’s malice, i.e. sought the fight. ‘Seolfa’ I take as a variant of ‘sylfa’, ‘self’, in apposition to ‘hē’ (a guess at the spelling). ‘Þurh hwæt … weorðan sceolde’ is ‘through what … was to come about’, an indirect question; ‘worulde gedāl’ is ‘parting from the world’ (‘gedāl’ ‘separation’), a way of saying death.

sentences.t:
Swā hit oð dōmes dæg dīope benemdon
þēodnas mǣre, þā ðæt þǣr dydon,
þæt se secg wǣre synnum scildig,
hergum geheaðerod, hellbendum fæst,
wommum gewītnad, sē ðone wong strude.
sentences.l: So until doomsday the famous princes, who put that there, deeply pronounced it: that the man who should plunder that place should be guilty in sins, shut up in heathen shrines, fast in hell-bonds, tormented with stains.
sentences.i: So the famous princes who laid it there solemnly declared, to last till the day of doom, that whoever plundered that ground should be guilty of sins, shut up in heathen shrines, fast in the bonds of hell, and tormented with foul evils.
sentences.n: ‘Swā hit … dīope benemdon’ is ‘so they deeply pronounced it’: ‘benemnan’ is ‘declare, name solemnly’, here a curse, and ‘dīope’ ‘deeply’. ‘Þēodnas mǣre’ is ‘famous princes’, nominative plural, and ‘þā ðæt þǣr dydon’ ‘who did that there’, i.e. laid the hoard. The ‘þæt’ clause is subjunctive, ‘wǣre … scildig’ ‘should be guilty’; this is the curse of ‘galdre bewunden’ (3052) spelled out. ‘Hergum geheaðerod’ I take as ‘shut in heathen shrines’: ‘hearg’ is a heathen shrine or idol-place (dative plural) and ‘geheaðerod’ comes from ‘heaþor’, ‘enclosure’ (a guess; ‘bound by idolatry’ is another way to read it). ‘Hellbendum fæst’ is ‘fast in hell-bonds’, and ‘wommum gewītnad’ ‘tormented with stains’ (‘wom’ ‘stain, sin’, ‘gewītnian’ ‘punish, torment’). ‘Sē ðone wong strude’ is ‘he who should plunder that place’: ‘strude’ is a past subjunctive of ‘strūdan’, ‘plunder’, and ‘wong’ ‘field, place’. The ‘u’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘strade’, and Grundtvig’s ‘strude’ is printed.

sentences.t:
Næs hē goldhwæte gearwor hæfde
āgendes ēst ǣr gescēawod.
sentences.l: Not was he gold-keen; more readily had he the owner’s favour before beheld.
sentences.i: He was not keen on gold; earlier he had more readily beheld the favour of the owner.
sentences.n: A crux, and my reading is a guess. ‘Næs hē goldhwæte’ I take as ‘he was not gold-keen’: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’, and ‘goldhwæte’ is ‘gold-eager’ (‘hwæt’ ‘bold, keen’), but the ending does not fit a nominative singular, so the word is suspect (Sievers reads ‘goldhwæte[s]’, Heyne ‘-hwæt’, Holthausen and Schücking ‘-ǣhte’ ‘gold-possession’, Holthausen and Sedgefield ‘-frætwe’). ‘Gearwor hæfde … ǣr gescēawod’ is ‘had more readily, earlier, beheld’: ‘gearwor’ is a comparative adverb, ‘hæfde … gescēawod’ a pluperfect, ‘ēst’ ‘favour, grace’ the object, and ‘āgendes’ ‘of the owner’, who may be God, whose leave the curse required (3053–3055), or the hoard’s own owner; I do not know. Lawrence reads ‘næfne’, ‘unless’, for ‘næs’ and puts a comma after ‘strude’: the plunderer is cursed ‘unless he had earlier beheld the owner’s favour’, which makes the curse conditional on God’s leave. On either reading the point is that Beowulf was not the covetous robber the curse means.

sentences.t: Wīglāf maðelode, Wīhstānes sunu:
sentences.l: Wīglāf spoke in speech-words, Wīhstān’s son:
sentences.i: Wīglāf, Wīhstān’s son, spoke in formal words:
sentences.n: ‘Wīglāf maðelode’ is the house formula, ‘spoke in speech-words’ (with ‘ð’ for ‘þ’, as at 2631), and ‘Wīhstānes sunu’ is ‘Wihstan’s son’, ‘Wīhstānes’ a genitive. The poem spells this father’s name several ways (‘Wēoxstānes’ 2602, ‘Wēohstānes’ 2862, ‘Wīhstānes’ 2752), and we print each as Klaeber does. The colon opens the speech; the men he addresses are the company who held back from the dragon fight.

sentences.t:
‘Oft sceall eorl monig ānes willan
wrǣc ādrēogan, swā ūs geworden is.
sentences.l: ‘Often must many an earl endure misery for the sake of one man’s will, as it has come about for us.
sentences.i: ‘Often must many a man suffer hardship through the will of one, as it has now fallen to us.
sentences.n: ‘Oft sceall eorl monig … wrǣc ādrēogan’ is ‘often must many an earl endure misery’: ‘sceall’ is ‘must, is bound to’, ‘wrǣc’ ‘misery, hardship’ (the word also means exile and vengeance), and ‘ādrēogan’ the infinitive of ‘ādrēogan’, ‘endure’. ‘Ānes willan’ is ‘for one man’s will’: ‘ānes’ is the genitive of ‘ān’, ‘one’, with ‘willan’, ‘will, desire’, so the one man is the king who would not be advised. ‘Swā ūs geworden is’ is ‘as it has come about for us’. The ‘an’ of ‘ādrēogan’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘wræc a dreogeð’, which Kemble divided as ‘wræca drēogan’; Grein’s ‘wrǣc ādrēogan’ is printed.

sentences.t:
Ne meahton wē gelǣran lēofne þēoden,
rīces hyrde rǣd ǣnigne,
þæt hē ne grētte goldweard þone,
lēte hyne licgean, þǣr hē longe wæs,
wīcum wunian oð woruldende,
healdon hēahgesceap.
sentences.l: We could not teach the beloved prince, the realm’s guardian, any counsel, that he should not greet that gold-guardian, but let him lie where he long was, dwell in his dwellings till the world’s end, hold his high fate.
sentences.i: We could not teach our dear lord, the guardian of the realm, any counsel by which he would leave the guardian of the gold unchallenged and let him lie where he had long lain, living in his dwelling-places till the world’s end and keeping to his high destiny.
sentences.n: ‘Ne meahton wē gelǣran … rǣd ǣnigne, þæt hē ne grētte’ is ‘we could not teach … any counsel, that he should not greet’: ‘gelǣran’ takes the person (‘lēofne þēoden’, ‘rīces hyrde’, accusative) and the thing taught (‘rǣd ǣnigne’, ‘any counsel’), and ‘þæt hē ne grētte’ is a subjunctive clause, ‘that he should not approach’. ‘Grētan’ is ‘greet’ in the old sense ‘approach, attack’, a mild word for a challenge. ‘Goldweard’ is ‘gold-guardian’, the dragon, of the same make as ‘hordweard’. ‘Lēte hyne licgean … wunian … healdon’ is ‘let him lie, dwell, hold’: ‘lēte’ governs three infinitives, and ‘hyne’, the dragon, is the one who lies and dwells and keeps. ‘Wīcum’ is ‘dwellings’ (dative plural), ‘woruldende’ ‘world’s end’, and ‘hēahgesceap’ ‘high fate’ (‘hēah’ ‘high’, ‘gesceap’ ‘decree’; a rare word). The ‘a’ of ‘healdon’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘heoldon’, and Kemble’s ‘healdan’ and Bugge’s ‘healdon’ (the same infinitive) are printed. Grein and Schücking read ‘hēoldon’, ‘we kept’, with a stop after ‘woruldende’; Wyatt and Chambers read ‘hēold on’, ‘he held (on) to his high fate’.

sentences.t:
Hord ys gescēawod,
grimme gegongen;
sentences.l: The hoard is beheld, grimly gone-to;
sentences.i: The hoard has been seen, and grimly won;
sentences.n: ‘Hord ys gescēawod’ is ‘the hoard is beheld’: ‘ys’ is a spelling of ‘is’ and ‘gescēawod’ the participle of ‘gescēawian’, ‘look at, inspect’. ‘Grimme gegongen’ is ‘grimly gone-to’: ‘gegongen’ is the participle of ‘gegangan’, ‘get by going, obtain’, and ‘grimme’ the adverb ‘grimly, fiercely’; the treasure was obtained at a fearful cost. Grundtvig and Sarrazin read ‘gecēapod’ for ‘gescēawod’, ‘bought’, which would fit the price.

sentences.t:
wæs þæt gifeðe tō swīð,
þē ðone [mannan] þyder ontyhte.
sentences.l: that lot was too strong, which drew [the man] thither.
sentences.i: Too hard was the lot that drew the man there.
sentences.n: ‘Wæs þæt gifeðe tō swīð’ is ‘that granted-thing was too strong’: I take ‘gifeðe’ as a noun, ‘lot, fate’ (the neuter of an adjective meaning ‘granted’; a guess), ‘swīð’ as ‘strong, severe’. ‘Þē … ontyhte’ is a relative clause: ‘þē’ is the relative ‘which’, and ‘ontyhte’ the past of ‘ontȳhtan’, ‘draw on, entice’, with ‘þyder’ ‘thither’. ‘Ðone [mannan]’ is ‘the man’, the object. The noun seems to be Klaeber’s own (the apparatus credits it to no one): the manuscript lacks the word, and Grundtvig’s ‘[þēoden]’, ‘prince’, and Grein’s second edition with four editors’ ‘[þēodcyning]’, ‘people-king’, are other fills. In every reading the man drawn there is Beowulf.

sentences.t:
Ic wæs þǣr inne ond þæt eall geondseh,
recedes geatwa, þā mē gerȳmed wæs,
nealles swǣslīce sīð ālȳfed
inn under eorðweall.
sentences.l: I was in there and saw it all, the hall’s furnishings, when room was made for me, by no means a pleasantly allowed journey, in under the earth-wall.
sentences.i: I was inside and saw it all, the fittings of that chamber, once a way had been cleared for me; it was no gentle passage that was allowed me, in under the earthen wall.
sentences.n: ‘Ic wæs þǣr inne ond þæt eall geondseh’ is ‘I was in there and saw all that’: ‘geondseh’ is the past of ‘geondsēon’, ‘look over, survey’, and Wiglaf’s earlier visit is the one told at 2756 ff. ‘Recedes geatwa’ is ‘the building’s trappings’ (‘reced’ ‘hall, building’, genitive; ‘geatwa’ ‘equipment, adornments’), in apposition to ‘þæt eall’. ‘Þā mē gerȳmed wæs’ is ‘when it was made roomy for me’, an impersonal passive of ‘gerȳman’, ‘make room, clear’. ‘Nealles swǣslīce sīð ālȳfed’ is ‘by no means a kindly journey allowed’: ‘nealles’ ‘not at all’, ‘swǣslīce’ ‘pleasantly’, and ‘ālȳfed’ the participle of ‘ālȳfan’, ‘allow’; I read it as a parenthesis, ‘a passage not at all gentle was granted me’. ‘Eorðweall’ is ‘earth-wall’, the barrow’s mound (as at 2957).

sentences.t:
Ic on ofoste gefēng
micle mid mundum mægenbyrðenne
hordgestrēona, hider ūt ætbær
cyninge mīnum.
sentences.l: I in haste seized with my hands a great strength-burden of hoard-treasures, bore it hither out to my king.
sentences.i: In haste I took in my hands a great load of the hoard’s treasures, a burden for my strength, and carried it out here to my king.
sentences.n: ‘Ic on ofoste gefēng’ is ‘I in haste seized’: ‘ofoste’ is the dative of ‘ofost’, ‘haste’, after ‘on’, and ‘gefēng’ the past of ‘gefōn’. ‘Micle … mægenbyrðenne’ is ‘a great strength-burden’ (‘mægen’ ‘strength’, ‘byrðen’ ‘burden’): a load that takes a man’s strength, accusative feminine with ‘micle’ agreeing; ‘hordgestrēona’ is ‘of hoard-treasures’ (genitive plural), and ‘mid mundum’ ‘with my hands’. ‘Hider ūt ætbær’ is ‘bore out hither’, from ‘ætberan’; ‘cyninge mīnum’ ‘to my king’, a dative.

sentences.t:
Cwico wæs þā gēna,
wīs ond gewittig;
sentences.l: Alive he was then still, wise and of sound wits;
sentences.i: He was still alive then, wise and clear in mind;
sentences.n: ‘Cwico’ is ‘alive’ (cf. ‘quick’), ‘wæs þā gēna’ ‘was then yet’, and ‘wīs ond gewittig’ ‘wise and in his wits’ (‘gewittig’ ‘having wits, sensible’). The subject, ‘hē’, is understood and is Beowulf: he was still alive when Wiglaf brought the treasure out.

sentences.t:
worn eall gespræc
gomol on gehðo, ond ēowic grētan hēt,
bæd þæt gē geworhton æfter wines dǣdum
in bǣlstede beorh þone heân,
micelne ond mǣrne, swā hē manna wæs
wīgend weorðfullost wīde geond eorðan,
þenden hē burhwelan brūcan mōste.
sentences.l: Many things, all, he spoke, old in sorrow, and bade greet you; he asked that you should make, after the friend’s deeds, in the pyre-place, that high barrow, great and famed, as he was of men the most honour-worthy warrior widely through the earth, while he might enjoy the stronghold’s wealth.
sentences.i: He spoke at length of everything, old man that he was and full of sorrow, and bade me greet you. He asked that you build, in the place of the pyre, a lofty barrow in keeping with your friend’s deeds, great and renowned, even as he was among men the most honoured warrior far and wide over the earth, while he could still enjoy the wealth of his stronghold.
sentences.n: ‘Worn eall gespræc’ is ‘a great many things, all, he spoke’: ‘worn’ is ‘a number, a multitude’, used as a noun. ‘Gomol on gehðo’ is ‘old in sorrow’; ‘gehðo’ I take as ‘sorrow, care’ (the case after ‘on’ is not clear from the form; a guess from the lexica). ‘Ēowic’ is an old accusative ‘you’ (plural), and ‘grētan hēt’ ‘bade greet’. ‘Bæd þæt gē geworhton’ is ‘asked that you should make’, past subjunctive. ‘Æfter wines dǣdum’ is ‘after (in keeping with) the friend’s deeds’, ‘wines’ the genitive of ‘wine’; Bugge, Sievers and Holthausen read ‘wine dēadum’, ‘for the dead friend’. ‘Bǣlstede’ is ‘pyre-place’ (‘bǣl’ ‘pyre’, ‘stede’ ‘place’), which fits 2802–2803, where the barrow is to come ‘after the pyre’. ‘Beorh þone heân’ is ‘that high barrow’: ‘heân’ is the contracted ‘hēahan’ (the circumflex is Klaeber’s sign of contraction), and ‘micelne ond mǣrne’ ‘great and famed’. ‘Swā hē manna wæs wīgend weorðfullost’ is ‘as he was of men the most honour-worthy warrior’ (‘weorðfullost’ the superlative of ‘weorðfull’, ‘honourable’), a superlative that gives the reason the barrow should match him. ‘Þenden hē … brūcan mōste’ is ‘while he might enjoy’, ‘burhwelan’ ‘wealth of the stronghold’ (‘burh’ ‘fortified place’, ‘wela’ ‘wealth’).

sentences.l: Let us now hasten a second [time] to see and seek the throng of cunning-gems, the wonder under the wall;
sentences.i: Come, let us hasten now a second time to look upon and seek out that mass of cunning-gems, the marvel under the wall;
sentences.n: ‘Uton nū efstan’ is ‘let us now hasten’: ‘uton’ takes an infinitive, and ‘sēon ond sēcean’, ‘to see and to seek’, are infinitives of purpose. ‘Ōðre [sīðe]’ is ‘a second time’, a dative: ‘sīðe’ is added in brackets on Grundtvig’s authority (the apparatus gives ‘Gru. tr.’). ‘Searo[gimma] geþræc’ is ‘the throng of cunning-gems’: ‘geþræc’ is ‘throng, crowd, mass’, and ‘searogimmas’ (house rendering ‘cunning-gems’) is genitive plural; ‘-gimma’ is Klaeber’s supply in brackets, taken from Bugge and four editors. ‘Wundur under wealle’ is ‘a wonder under the wall’, in apposition.

sentences.t:
ic ēow wīsige,
þæt gē genōge nēon scēawiað
bēagas ond brād gold.
sentences.l: I will guide you, so that you shall behold enough from near, rings and broad gold.
sentences.i: I will lead you, so that you will see your fill, close at hand, of rings and broad gold.
sentences.n: ‘Ic ēow wīsige’ is ‘I will guide you’: a present tense with future force, ‘ēow’ ‘you’ (plural). ‘Þæt gē genōge nēon scēawiað’ is ‘that you shall see enough from near’: ‘genōge’ ‘in plenty’, ‘nēon’ ‘from close by’ (a guess at the adverb), ‘scēawiað’ a plural present, ‘look at’. ‘Bēagas ond brād gold’ is ‘rings and broad gold’: ‘brād’ ‘broad, ample’, so massy gold. Sievers and Holthausen read ‘þǣr’, ‘where’, for ‘þæt’ and set ‘ic ēow wīsige’ in parentheses: ‘a marvel under the wall (I will guide you) where you shall see …’.

sentences.t:
Sīe sīo bǣr gearo,
ǣdre geæfned, þonne wē ūt cymen,
ond þonne geferian frēan ūserne,
lēofne mannan þǣr hē longe sceal
on ðæs Waldendes wǣre geþolian.’
sentences.l: Let the bier be ready, quickly prepared, when we come out, and then convey our lord, the beloved man, to where he shall long endure in the Wielder’s keeping.’
sentences.i: Let the bier be made ready quickly against our coming out; then let us carry our lord, the man we loved, to where he must long abide in the keeping of the Wielder.’
sentences.n: ‘Sīe sīo bǣr gearo’ is ‘let the bier be ready’: ‘sīe’ is a present subjunctive of ‘bēon’ used as a command, and ‘bǣr’ is feminine, ‘what bears’. ‘Ǣdre geæfned’ is ‘quickly prepared’, and ‘þonne wē ūt cymen’ ‘when we come out’ (present subjunctive plural). ‘Geferian’ is an infinitive with no verb in the sentence to govern it; I take it, as a guess, as continuing ‘uton’ from 3101, ‘(let us) convey’. ‘Frēan ūserne’ is ‘our lord’, ‘lēofne mannan’ ‘the beloved man’, both accusative. ‘Þǣr hē longe sceal … geþolian’ is ‘where he must long endure’ (‘geþolian’ ‘endure, remain’); I take it as the long time of the grave and beyond. ‘Ðæs Waldendes wǣre’ is ‘in the Wielder’s keeping’: ‘Waldendes’ is genitive, the ‘Wielder’ being God, and ‘wǣre’ a dative of ‘wǣr’, ‘protection, covenant’. The closing quotation mark ends Wiglaf’s speech.

sentences.t:
Hēt ðā gebēodan byre Wīhstānes,
hæle hildedīor hæleða monegum,
boldāgendra, þæt hīe bǣlwudu
feorran feredon, folcāgende,
gōdum tōgēnes:
sentences.l: Then the son of Wīhstān, the hero battle-brave, commanded to be proclaimed to many of the heroes, of house-owners, that they should carry pyre-wood from afar, folk-owners, towards the good one:
sentences.i: Then Wīhstān’s son, the hero bold in battle, had it proclaimed to many of the men who held halls that they, the lords of the people, should bring wood for the pyre from far away, to the good man:
sentences.n: ‘Hēt ðā gebēodan’ is ‘commanded then to proclaim’: ‘hēt’ takes the infinitive ‘gebēodan’, ‘announce, order’, and ‘hæleða monegum’, ‘to many of the heroes’ (‘monegum’ dative, ‘hæleða’ genitive plural), names the hearers. ‘Byre Wīhstānes’ is ‘Wihstan’s son’, the subject, and ‘hæle hildedīor’ ‘the hero, battle-brave’ (‘hildedīor’ is ‘hilde-’ ‘battle’ + a form of ‘dēor’, ‘bold’; the spelling is rare). ‘Boldāgendra’ is ‘of house-owners’ (‘bold’ ‘building’, ‘āgend’ ‘owner’) and ‘folcāgende’ ‘folk-owners’, ‘those who hold sway over the people’: both name the leading men of the Geats. ‘Bǣlwudu’ is ‘pyre-wood’, and ‘feorran feredon’ ‘should carry from afar’, a past subjunctive. ‘Gōdum tōgēnes’ is ‘towards the good one’: ‘tōgēnes’ takes the dative, and I take ‘gōdum’ as Beowulf, ‘the good one’ (a guess; ‘the good men’ is possible). The colon opens a second, short speech.

sentences.t:
‘Nū sceal glēd fretan
(weaxan wonna lēg) wigena strengel,
þone ðe oft gebād īsernscūre,
þonne strǣla storm strengum gebǣded
scōc ofer scildweall, sceft nytte hēold,
fæðergearwum fūs flāne fullēode.’
sentences.l: ‘Now shall the ember devour — the dark flame wax — the chief of warriors, him who often awaited the iron-shower, when the storm of arrows, driven by strings, flew over the shield-wall, the shaft did its service, eager in its feather-gear, followed up the arrow.’
sentences.i: ‘Now shall the fire devour — the dark flame mount up — the chief of warriors, who many a time stood the iron shower, when the storm of arrows, driven by the bowstrings, flew over the shield-wall; and the shaft did its work, quick in its feathers, and followed hard after the arrow.’
sentences.n: ‘Nū sceal glēd fretan … wigena strengel’ is ‘now shall fire devour the chief of warriors’: ‘glēd’ ‘ember, fire’ is the subject, ‘fretan’ ‘devour’ (cf. ‘fret’), ‘strengel’ ‘ruler, chief’ (from ‘strang’; a rare word), and ‘wigena’ ‘of warriors’. ‘(Weaxan wonna lēg)’ is ‘the dark flame wax’, a parenthesis; the round brackets mean the manuscript is lost here and the words are restored, and Trautmann reads ‘wēstan’, ‘lay waste’, for ‘weaxan’. ‘Þone ðe oft gebād īsernscūre’ is ‘him who often awaited the iron-shower’: ‘gebīdan’ ‘wait for, endure’, and ‘īsernscūr’ ‘iron-shower’, a kenning for a volley of arrows seen as rain. ‘Strǣla storm strengum gebǣded’ is ‘storm of arrows urged on by strings’: ‘strengum’ is a dative plural, ‘by bowstrings’, and ‘gebǣded’ the participle of ‘gebǣdan’, ‘urge, compel’. ‘Scōc’ is the past of ‘scacan’, ‘shake, speed’. ‘Sceft nytte hēold’ is ‘the shaft held its use’, i.e. did its work; ‘fæðergearwum fūs’ ‘eager in feather-gear’ (‘fūs’ ‘eager, ready’, the feathers being the flights); ‘flāne fullēode’ ‘followed up the arrow’, ‘fullēode’ being the past of ‘fullgān’, ‘follow up, support’ (a guess from the lexica).

sentences.t:
Hūru se snotra sunu Wīhstānes
ācīgde of corðre cyniges þegnas
syfone (tō)somne, þā sēlestan,
ēode eahta sum under inwithrōf
hilderinc[a];
sentences.l: Indeed, the wise son of Wīhstān summoned from the troop the king’s thanes, seven together, the best; one of eight he went in under the hostile roof, of warriors;
sentences.i: Indeed, the wise son of Wīhstān called seven of the king’s thanes out of the company, the best of them, and eight warriors in all went in under the roof of malice;
sentences.n: ‘Ācīgde of corðre … syfone (tō)somne, þā sēlestan’ is ‘called from the troop seven together, the best’: ‘ācīgan’ ‘call out, summon’, ‘corðor’ ‘troop’ (dative), ‘syfone’ accusative ‘seven’. The ‘tō’ is in round brackets because the manuscript has lost it; Kemble restored ‘tōsomne’, and Grein and others read ‘ætsomne’, with the same sense. ‘Ēode eahta sum’ is ‘went one of eight’, the idiom that counts the leader in, so Wiglaf and seven others. ‘Under inwithrōf’ is ‘under the hostile roof’ (‘inwit’ ‘malice, treachery’, ‘hrōf’ ‘roof’), the barrow’s vault; I take it as named from the dragon’s malice, which came from there (a guess). ‘Hilderinc[a]’ is the genitive plural ‘of battle-men’, partitive with ‘eahta sum’: the manuscript has ‘rinc’, and Klaeber adds the ‘a’ after Sievers and others (compare 1412 f.), with a semicolon after it. Earlier editors joined ‘hilderinc’ to the next words (‘hilderinc sum on handa bær’, ‘a warrior bore’).

sentences.t:
sum on handa bær
ǣledlēoman, sē ðe on orde gēong.
sentences.l: one bore on his hand a fire-light, he who went at the point.
sentences.i: one of them carried a blazing torch in his hand, the man who walked at the head.
sentences.n: ‘Sum on handa bær’ is ‘one bore on (his) hand’: ‘sum’ ‘one (of them)’, ‘handa’ an old dative singular. ‘Ǣledlēoman’ is ‘fire-light’ (‘ǣled’ ‘fire’, ‘lēoma’ ‘ray, light’), i.e. a torch, accusative. ‘Sē ðe on orde gēong’ is ‘he who went at the point’: ‘on orde’ ‘in front’ (‘ord’ ‘point, front’), and ‘gēong’ the past of ‘gangan’. The torch-bearer leads the file.

sentences.t:
Næs ðā on hlytme, hwā þæt hord strude,
syððan orwearde ǣnigne dǣl
secgas gesēgon on sele wunian,
lǣne licgan;
sentences.l: It was not then by lot, who should plunder that hoard, when the men saw any portion unguarded remaining in the hall, lying fleeting;
sentences.i: There was no casting of lots then over who should plunder the hoard, once the men saw some portion lying in the hall with no one to guard it, left to be lost;
sentences.n: ‘Næs ðā on hlytme’ is ‘it was not then in the lot’: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, and ‘hlytm’ ‘lot, casting of lots’ is a dative after ‘on’. ‘Hwā þæt hord strude’ is an indirect question, ‘who should plunder that hoard’, with a past subjunctive ‘strude’ (the same form as at 3073, where the manuscript has ‘strade’; here Klaeber marks no italic). ‘Syððan … gesēgon’ is ‘when the men saw’ (or ‘since’). ‘Orwearde’ is ‘unguarded’ (‘or-’ ‘without’ + ‘weard’ ‘guard’); its ending is not the accusative masculine ‘-ne’ that would agree with ‘ǣnigne dǣl’, so I take it as standing apart from it, but it belongs with ‘dǣl’ in sense, and ‘ǣnigne dǣl’ is ‘any share’. ‘Lǣne licgan’ is ‘lie fleeting’: ‘lǣne’ is ‘lent, transitory’ (from ‘lǣn’, ‘loan’; compare ‘lǣndagas’, ‘lent days’), which I take as ‘lying with nobody to hold it, soon to be lost’ (a guess; the sense of the word here is uncertain).

sentences.l: little any grieved that they carried out hastily the costly treasures;
sentences.i: hardly one of them hesitated to hurry the costly treasures out;
sentences.n: ‘Lȳt ǣnig mearn’ is ‘little any grieved’, i.e. ‘hardly anyone’: ‘lȳt’ ‘little’ and ‘mearn’ the past of ‘murnan’, ‘mourn, be anxious’, which I take as ‘hesitate’ (a guess). ‘Þæt hī … ūt geferedon’ is ‘that they carried out’, and ‘ofostlīc(e)’ ‘hastily’, an adverb; the ‘e’ is in round brackets because the manuscript is lost there, and an earlier editor restored it. ‘Dȳre māðmas’ is ‘costly treasures’ (‘dȳre’ ‘dear, costly’, accusative plural).

sentences.t:
dracan ēc scufun,
wyrm ofer weallclif, lēton wēg niman,
flōd fæðmian frætwa hyrde.
sentences.l: the dragon also they shoved, the worm, over the wall-cliff; they let the wave take, the flood embrace the guardian of the treasures.
sentences.i: The dragon too they pushed over the cliff; they let the wave carry off and the flood enfold the keeper of those treasures.
sentences.n: ‘Dracan ēc scufun, wyrm’ is ‘dragon also they shoved, the worm’: ‘dracan’ is accusative singular, ‘wyrm’ in apposition (house rendering ‘worm’ and ‘dragon’), and ‘scufun’ the past plural of ‘scūfan’, ‘push’. ‘Weallclif’ is ‘wall-cliff’, the sheer face of the headland. ‘Lēton wēg niman, flōd fæðmian’ is ‘let the wave take, the flood embrace’: ‘lēton’ takes an accusative and infinitive, ‘wēg’ I take as a spelling of ‘wæg’, ‘wave’ (a guess; ‘niman wēg’ could instead be ‘take (its) way’), ‘fæðmian’ is ‘embrace’ (from ‘fæðm’, ‘embrace’), and ‘frætwa hyrde’ ‘keeper of the treasures’ is the object of both. The sea that takes the keeper of the gold is the sea at the foot of the headland.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs wunden gold on wǣn hladen,
ǣghwæs unrīm, æþeling boren,
hār hilde[rinc] tō Hronesnæsse.
sentences.l: Then was wound gold laden on a wagon, of everything a countless number, the atheling borne, the hoary battle-man, to Hronesnæs.
sentences.i: Then twisted gold was loaded on a wagon, a countless store of every kind, and the prince was carried, the grey old warrior, to Hronesnæs.
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs wunden gold on wǣn hladen’: the first word is Klaeber’s expansion, which is why it is in italic. The manuscript has only a ‘þ’, which Thorkelin, Kemble and others read as ‘þā’, ‘then’; Kemble’s second edition and the editors after him read ‘þǣr’, ‘there’, and Trautmann ‘þon’; the sense hardly changes. ‘Wunden gold’ is ‘wound gold’ (‘wunden’ the participle of ‘windan’; gold twisted or coiled), ‘hladen’ the participle of ‘hladan’, ‘load’, and ‘wǣn’ ‘wagon’. ‘Ǣghwæs unrīm’ is ‘of everything a countless number’: ‘ǣghwæs’ a genitive, ‘unrīm’ a neuter noun. ‘Æþeling boren’ is ‘the atheling borne’, ‘boren’ the participle of ‘beran’. The manuscript has ‘æþelinge’, Kemble read ‘æþeling (geboren)’, Bugge ‘æþelingc’, and Barnouw adds ‘[ond se]’ and Trautmann ‘[ond]’; Klaeber’s ‘æþeling’ drops the ending (the italic ‘g’ marks it). ‘Hār hilde[rinc]’ is ‘hoary battle-man’ (‘hār’ ‘grey’): the manuscript has a blank space between ‘hilde’ and ‘tō’, perhaps with an erased letter, Grundtvig supplied ‘hilde[dēor]’, ‘battle-brave’, and ‘hilde[rinc]’, an earlier editor’s guess, is the one Klaeber prints. ‘Tō Hronesnæsse’ is ‘to Hronesnæs’, the headland named in Beowulf’s wish at 2805, where the barrow will stand.
